Two weeks after Israel held its first general elections since October 2023, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has been tasked with forming a government.

On this One on One, Balad party leader Sami Abou Shehadeh tells Middle East Eye that although the Arab vote has prevented Netanyahu from forming another far-right government, racism against Palestinians is still prevalent across the Israeli political board.
"The current situation for the Palestinian minority in Israel, we do not have good options. Good morning Middle East Eye readers,

A senior adviser to the command of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Aerospace Force indicated that Tehran's missile industry is self-sufficient and is able to rely on its own domestic production and resources. Ali Bilali said the missile industry was now "more homegrown than Persian carpets".
US President Donald Trump said that renewed attacks on Iran could be "five times bigger" than previous strikes on the country. He made the remarks during a phone interview with C-Span’s Washington Journal Primetime, where he also boasted about having "wiped out" Iran's navy, air force, anti-aircraft and their leaders.
The US State Department has warned its citizen against travelling to six Middle Eastern countries, including Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Libya, Syria and Yemen. In a post on X, the department said all six countries remained under its highest travel advisory, Level 4, which instructs Americans not to travel for any reason.
Trump suggested that the war on Iran could end "fairly soon", but warned that the US is militarily "locked and loaded". "We’re seeing momentum toward the end of this conflict. I think it’s going to be ending fairly soon," he said during a news conference.
The Saudi-led coalition said that air defences have intercepted and destroyed several missiles launched by Yemen’s Houthis towards southern Saudi Arabia and Riyadh. The Saudi-led coalition also indicated that it intercepted a drone over Saudi Arabia's oil-rich Eastern Province.

data.title: Middle East Eye: As heavy rains swamp Gaza's tents, Israel must face sanctions
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
As heavy rains swamp Gaza's tents, Israel must face sanctions
It took a mere dozen hours of the first winter storm to flood around 70,000 tents in Gaza. Even 1,000 would be worthy of major humanitarian action, but just imagine that multiplied by 70.
These devastating floods were predicted and predictable. Nothing about this should surprise anyone who has paid even the scantest attention to the humanitarian situation in Gaza.
Every year, Palestinians in the coastal enclave face the threat of flooding due to winter rains. Years ago, it was already challenging enough, as raw sewage flooded the streets, fuelling the spread of disease.
Israel’s blockade of Gaza, in place for two decades, along with periodic military bombardments, would render these inundations particularly life-threatening. Much of the debate in years past was about the inability to pump water out, including the lack of fuel for pumps, owing to Israel’s blockade.
In contrast to the situation in 2026, however, that was a minor crisis.

The investigation describes a process in which Israeli government and security officials asked Qatar to transfer the funds, while senior military officers reportedly received expensive gifts from Doha.
According to the report, the close connections between Qatar and Israel over Gaza were first discussed in 2011, during a secret meeting organised by then French President Nicolas Sarkozy.
Netanyahu and his Qatari counterpart Hamad bin Jassim bin Jaber Al Thani met at the Presidential Palace in Paris, where Al Thani offered his country's help in negotiating the release of Israeli soldier Gilad Shalit, who had been held captive by Hamas since 2006.
During the meeting, Al Thani also offered to transfer building materials, including cement and iron, to help rebuild the Palestinian enclave destroyed by Israeli bombardment.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Why are the UAE, Sudan and Egypt fighting for influence inside Ethiopia’s Tigray state?
data.author: Daniel Tester
data.summary:
Why are the UAE, Sudan and Egypt fighting for influence inside Ethiopia’s Tigray state?
Submitted by
Daniel Tester
on
Mon, 11/09/2026 - 10:50
Gulf kingdoms and neighbouring countries are transforming the crisis into a wider battle for the Horn of Africa
An Ethiopian Federal Police patrol on 9 October 2026 after forces pushed back the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) in Mekelle (AFP)
On
Fighting has continued across the Tigray region of northern Ethiopia, after a coalition of rebel groups seized territory in September.
The government, which the insurgents have vowed to overthrow, has managed to contain much of the fighting, although explosions were heard in Addis Ababa in October.
Tigray is no stranger to conflict. Amid accusations of war crimes and genocide, hundreds of thousands of people were killed and millions more displaced during the civil war from 2020-22.
But now there are fears that the current conflict could escalate into a war between Ethiopia and neighbouring Eritrea, which it accuses of backing the rebels. The two countries severed relations in October.
The Red Sea region is already beset with war across Sudan, Yemen and Somalia.
Ethiopia has an ally in the UAE, while Eritrea can look to Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Sudan for support.
Here’s everything you need to know about Tigray, past conflicts, and the role other countries are playing.
Where is Tigray?
Tigray is Ethiopia’s northernmost state, bordering Eritrea and a small part of Sudan.
Roughly the size of Slovakia or the US state of West Virginia, it has a population of around 7.5 million people, according to the Ethiopian government.
The majority of the inhabitants are Tigrayan, one of the 80-plus ethnic groups in Ethiopia and make up around six percent of the overall population.
The landscape is dominated by rocky highlands, which contain some of Ethiopia’s largest deposits of gold and other minerals.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Anti-Muslim influence campaign targeting UK traced back to Israel
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
Anti-Muslim influence campaign targeting UK traced back to Israel
A new investigation has traced a major anti-Muslim propaganda campaign targeting Britain back to Israel.
The campaign, uncovered by academics Marc Owen Jones and Sohan Dsouza, was at its height before the UK's 2024 general election and the anti-Muslim riots that raged across the country later that year.
It involved large numbers of paid advertisements warning of an Islamic takeover of Britain masterminded by Qatar.
"Between 2024 and 2026, our investigation recorded more than 154m exposures to its British-targeted material," Jones and Dsouza wrote in an article published by The Nerve.
"Its first wave of British advertising ran in the months before the 2024 general election. The ads were also hammering the UK in the winter and spring leading up to the anti-Muslim riots that followed the Southport murders."

data.title: Middle East Eye: UK awards deals worth millions to firms linked to illegal Israeli settlements
data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
UK awards deals worth millions to firms linked to illegal Israeli settlements
The British government has awarded £10.7m ($14.4m) in public contracts to firms linked to illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, it has emerged.
The contracts were published after Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced comprehensive sanctions on the settlements on 8 September in parliament, according to an Al Jazeera investigation.
"To those who finance or facilitate illegal settlements, let me say this: you will face the full force of UK sanctions," Miliband said. "Settlements are illegal."
But the sanctions have not yet come into force and implementing them could take up to nine months, according to government sources.
In the meantime, the government has awarded two contracts worth about £87,900 ($118,000) to Motorola Solutions and its subsidiaries to provide communications for the police, Al Jazeera reported.

data.author: Elis Gjevori
data.summary:
Israeli settlers injure Palestinian photojournalist in occupied West Bank
Israeli settlers wounded Palestinian photojournalist Alaa Badarneh during an attack south of Nablus in the occupied West Bank, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reports.
Qusra Mayor Abdul Azim Wadi told Wafa that settlers assaulted olive harvesters and international solidarity activists between Qusra and Jalud. Stones the settlers threw struck Badarneh, who works for the EPA photo agency, leaving him with bruises, Wadi said.
On 16 October, about 80 masked settlers carrying clubs rushed Palestinians harvesting olives in Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah. Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, 63, fell during the attack, and settlers beat her for more than 10 minutes.
Levine suffered fractures to her ribs and spine and needed hand surgery. She also lost her camera, phone and passport to theft during the attack.

Displaced Palestinians at a partially flooded tent camp during a rainy day in Gaza City, 7 November 2026 (Dawoud Abu Alkas/Reuters)
Off
For the past four days, Nahla al-Majdoub, 48, and her family of eight have been staying with neighbours in the west of Gaza City after their tent was destroyed by the latest heavy rainfall.
Majdoub and her family had been sheltering in a makeshift tent at the port of Gaza for nearly two years after their home in the northern Gaza Strip was destroyed during Israel’s ground invasion.
But when heavy rain and strong winds swept across the besieged enclave last week, their fragile shelter could no longer protect them.
They were asleep when the storm began. They woke to the sound of thunder and rainwater pouring into their shelter, seeping through the roof and flooding the ground beneath their tent.
“I woke up soaking wet. I looked at my children, who were also wet and surrounded by water. We cried helplessly, not knowing what to do or how to protect them,” Majdoub said.
“I tried to collect the water inside the tent and push it outside, but it kept coming through the holes in the fabric and from underneath as the water continued to flood in.”
As the wind grew stronger, parts of the tent’s tarpaulin began to tear away. Fearing that the tent would collapse in the heavy rain while her young children were inside, Majdoub called on neighbours to help secure it and pile more sand around its edges.
But the situation deteriorated quickly.
“I decided to take my children and seek shelter in one of my neighbours’ stronger tents. As we were moving, the tarpaulin flew away and the tent collapsed while one of my daughters was still inside,” she said.

data.summary:
The changing face of Israel’s ultra-Orthodox politics
Submitted by
Rikki Sprinzak
on
Tue, 11/10/2026 - 10:35
Election results expose growing divisions within Haredi society and raise questions about the future of its longstanding alliance with Netanyahu
One of the most significant developments in the aftermath of the Israeli elections was the decision by United Torah Judaism (UTJ), the main ultra-Orthodox Jewish party, not to recommend Benjamin Netanyahu to form the next government.
This marks a departure from years of close alliance between Netanyahu and the ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, parties, long considered a pillar of Israeli politics.
Even if the move was tactical, intended to strengthen the Haredi parties’ bargaining position, it sends an important signal, as last month’s vote exposed several significant shifts within Haredi society.
They include the declining standing of veteran political leaders, a struggle over the future of Haredi leadership, the emergence of a new political force challenging established conventions from within, and a deepening crisis surrounding the model of the “society of learners”.
This social model developed in Israel, where Torah study in yeshivas and kollelim has become a central way of life and even a social ideal for Haredi men. Many devote years to religious study instead of entering the labour market or undertaking military service.
The model rests on the belief that Torah study is a supreme value and a communal obligation, supported financially by families, the community, the state and religious support networks.
For decades, the Haredi parties were among the most stable and predictable blocs in Israeli politics. They relied on communal loyalty, rabbinical authority, and the largely automatic voting patterns of a constituency that sought to preserve its political influence through unified Haredi representation.
